title: Determination Pursuant to Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, as Amended
summary:
The Department of Homeland Security has announced it will waive a wide range of laws to speed the construction of new border barriers and roads along a stretch of the New Mexico border near El Paso, effective October 8, 2025. In a separate notice, the Federal Railroad Administration corrected an online listing for a nationwide intercity passenger rail grant and confirmed applications are due by January 7, 2026.

Homeland Security says the New Mexico area is a high-traffic zone for illegal crossings and drug smuggling, citing more than 1.2 million apprehensions since 2021. The waivers cover many environmental, wildlife, historic preservation, land management, and administrative laws to allow construction to move forward quickly with fencing, roads, lighting, and cameras. The agency points to long-standing authority from Congress and a recent presidential order to justify acting now.

Those who stand to benefit most from the border decision include Border Patrol and neighboring communities that want faster construction to deter unlawful crossings and improve response times. Contractors and suppliers connected to the project may also see work move ahead sooner. On the rail notice, state and local transportation agencies, passenger rail operators, and their partners benefit from clarity on how to apply and when, which helps them keep projects on track.

Those who might be negatively affected by the border decision include nearby residents, landowners, and tribal and cultural groups who could lose chances for public input or consultation because normal review steps are being set aside. Wildlife and sensitive habitats along the construction path may face more immediate impacts without the usual environmental studies and safeguards. The waivers also limit opportunities for legal challenges, which some view as reducing transparency. For the rail grant, the impact is minimal, though applicants who miss the corrected listing could face confusion if they do not adjust in time.
